posts.body_html:
Beautiful MW. The attractive traits of the clone are holding nice and firm. Well worthy of the name of your special lovely friend!

Has the clone been grown in a green house yet? Interested to know if it takes on a different appearance under those conditions or stays the same.

In any event, I believe outdoor colouration is where its at. In fact, although it'll never happen I'm sure, I tend to believe outdoor colouration should possibly be the standard for cultivars rather than all the anomalous colours that can be delivered up under the artificial light diffusion provided by green house cladding, especially, plastic. Essentially the description being founded on: What is the natural colouration delivered by the genetics of the plant as grown under natural sunshine? What do you think on that?

posts.body_html:
Interesting idea KE! This hasn't yet been grown under greenhouse conditions,but I would expect the lid to turn whiter, and perhaps the body could turn a darker red.

As for using outdoor conditions as metrics for cultivar descriptions, it seems the results can be equally variable and anomalous. For example, If you look at S. x Adrian Slack when it was growing outdoors at Bob Hanrahan's property in Alabama, the colors were way more intense than anything I've ever seen elsewhere, outdoors or indoors. Also, plants in nature produce some of the best colors you can find.

I scratch my head on your question because under your and my outdoor, mediterranian climate, the colors can become intense, but it's not as intense as under a greenhouse at the same latitude. However, go to the SE US, and outdoor colors can be good as what you get in a greenhouse, if not better.

I guess I'm thinking of close to the degree of light that the plants are adapted for (as you point out, our respective locations relatively approximate natural Sarra habitat) rather than marginal cultivation conditions that some growers have no choice but to work with. Any-which-way, I love outdoor colours. They look soothingly natural to my eye backed by the direct relationship between the sun's rays and the plants.

Reminded by these questions on growing it elsewhere, I've been meaning to ask: it 'Elaine Wang' a vigorous hybrid? I know 'Adrian Slack' is a notoriously slow grower, but 'Judith Hindle' is the very opposite, often very robust in its growth. Which one does it follow closer in that respect, or is it more like in the middle?
I still can't get over the superbly perfect contrast in colors this thing has.....

Jan 12, 2014 0:53:20 GMT -5 hcarlton said:
Reminded by these questions on growing it elsewhere, I've been meaning to ask: it 'Elaine Wang' a vigorous hybrid? I know 'Adrian Slack' is a notoriously slow grower, but 'Judith Hindle' is the very opposite, often very robust in its growth. Which one does it follow closer in that respect, or is it more like in the middle?
I still can't get over the superbly perfect contrast in colors this thing has.....


Hi Hcarlton,

New divisions seem to have medium vigor. However, once it has momentum and the plant is established, it seems to take off and grow pretty fast. By no means would I call this plant a slow grower, but it's not the fastest: somewhere in between Adrian Slack and Judith Hindle is pretty accurate.


Nelio-Thank you for the compliment! In reality, breeding this plant was more dumb luck than anything. I rarely make hybrid crosses, but just happen to do this one, and one of them turned out to be out of this world. In fact, I neglected the seed batch for many years, and almost killed them off! Interestingly enough, even as baby, when S. x Elaine Wang produced its first adult pitcher, you could tell this plant was special. I just didn't know it would be even more amazing as it grew up...

ocpaddict-glad you like the S. x Elaine Wang siblings! I've had others (ie. Phil Faulisi, the master hybridizer) think some of them are worth registering as well, and they're now exclusive to other people's collections No doubt, many have great breeding potential.
